<!--
  PMS 1.43.3 GET /library/sections/{key}/all?type=1&unwatched=0&includeGuids=1 — the SAME watched
  read `plex_pms.watched_titles` already makes, recorded once per token to show what `userRating`
  does across accounts. Recorded 2026-08-06 from a real server (plex-safety rule 11). Titles, ids,
  summaries and account names are sanitized; attribute NAMES, ordering, value FORMAT and the
  container shape are verbatim.

  WHY THIS FIXTURE EXISTS.

  Issue #69 asks for a viewer's own rating to stop a title seeding their row. That turns on three
  claims about this response, none of which had ever been measured:

    1. `userRating` is returned by the read we ALREADY make — no second request, no new endpoint.
    2. It is scoped to the TOKEN, not the server, so one person's opinion cannot reach another's row.
    3. Its value tells you what the person actually thought.

  WHAT WAS MEASURED, across all 50 accounts on the server (owner + 49 shared):

    1. TRUE.  `userRating` rides along on `/library/sections/{k}/all`, costing nothing.
    2. TRUE.  1,462 titles carried a `userRating` as the owner and NO `userRating` at all for every
              one of the 49 viewers. Per-account, confirmed by disagreement, not by assumption.
    3. FALSE for the owner, TRUE for the viewers — and that is what this fixture is really for.

  THE TRAP (rows 1-2 below).

  The owner's account had 1,455 of 1,630 watched titles rated, and 90.7% of those values were
  FRACTIONAL — 7.9, 8.8, 6.2. Plex's own controls cannot write those: stars move in half-star steps
  on a 0..10 scale, and thumbs land on the same grid, so every value a PERSON can produce is a whole
  number. An external tool wrote these (Kometa's rating sync copies IMDb/TMDB scores into the field;
  note row 2, where `userRating` equals `rating` exactly). `lastRatedAt` gives it away independently:
  the owner's three sampled ratings are stamped 1696072109, 1696072110 and 1696070087 — two of them
  one second apart, which is a bulk write, not an opinion.

  Across the 49 real viewers, by contrast, 0 of 36 ratings were fractional.

  So a naive `userRating <= threshold` would have read IMDb's opinion as the OWNER's and silently
  stopped dozens of their own seeds. `WatchedItem.is_human_rating` is the guard, and row 1 is the
  case it exists to reject: a fractional value that a person could never have entered.

  ROW 1 also carries the residue the per-value guard CANNOT catch: `userRating="6.0"` on row 3 is
  tool-written too, and is a whole number. That is why the account-level guard in `history.py`
  exists as a second layer — see `_ratings_are_trustworthy`.

  THE HONEST CASE (rows 4-5). A viewer's rating: whole-numbered, and `lastRatedAt` sits a few
  minutes after `lastViewedAt` — someone finished a film and rated it. Row 5 is the shape the
  feature acts on, a low rating from a real person.

  ROW 6 is the overwhelming majority: watched, never rated, no `userRating` attribute at all. 99.7%
  of watched rows on this server look like this, so "absent" is the case to optimise for.

  NOTE: no `totalSize` on this container — see `watched_titles`, which treats a short page as the
  only end-signal when the server omits it.
-->
